evals.prompt: Write the production runbook for 'order-svc', the order-processing service of our 'Cartwheel' e-commerce platform. Context you can use: it's owned by the Fulfillment team (on-call rotation exists with primary/secondary); architecture is described in SAD v3.2 (order-svc consumes from Kafka topic orders.incoming, writes to Postgres, calls the payment gateway); known failure modes are Kafka consumer lag, Postgres connection-pool exhaustion, and payment-gateway timeouts; alerts already defined are OrderQueueAgeHigh, OrderSvcDbPoolSaturated, and PaymentGatewayErrorRateHigh; NFR-012 sets RTO 4h / RPO 15min and an SLO of 99.9% successful order processing. Deployment is via Helm on Kubernetes with a blue/green switch. Make it something a brand-new on-call engineer could follow at 3am.
evals.expected_output: A runbook following the ten-section structure: document control with review cadence; service overview and Fulfillment-team ownership; an architecture summary that links SAD v3.2 rather than restating it; dependencies (Kafka, Postgres, payment gateway) with how each fails; monitoring covering all three named alerts with meaning and first action each; standard operating procedures (deploy, scale, restart, secret rotation); incident-response procedures per known failure mode; an explicit escalation path with primary/secondary and time thresholds; rollback/recovery tied to the RTO 4h / RPO 15min from NFR-012; and appendices — every step concrete enough for a stranger to execute.
expectations: The runbook contains all ten recommended sections, including Document Control (version, authors, status, review cadence) and Appendices (dashboards, log queries, related ADRs)
The Architecture Summary links/references SAD v3.2 instead of redefining the topology
Dependencies & Failure Modes covers Kafka, Postgres, and the payment gateway, stating how each dependency fails
Every one of the three named alerts (OrderQueueAgeHigh, OrderSvcDbPoolSaturated, PaymentGatewayErrorRateHigh) appears with what it means and a defined first action

Steps are executable by someone unfamiliar with the system: concrete commands (e.g. kubectl/Helm/systemctl/SQL) with a verification step (e.g. health endpoint or metric to confirm recovery), never 'restart the service' alone
Standard Operating Procedures cover routine tasks including deploy (blue/green via Helm), scale, restart, and secret rotation
There is an incident-response procedure for each of the three known failure modes (consumer lag, pool exhaustion, gateway timeouts)
The escalation path is explicit: primary and secondary on-call named/roled, with a time threshold for escalating further — not 'ping the team'
Rollback/recovery procedures cite the RTO of 4h and RPO of 15min from NFR-012 rather than inventing ad hoc targets

evals.prompt: Leadership said every service needs a runbook by end of month. I maintain 'geo-tiler', a map-tile rendering service someone else built years ago. I honestly don't know what alerts exist for it, whether it has SLO targets, who's on call for it, or where its architecture is documented — I just know it runs on two VMs and restarting it usually fixes things. Write me the runbook anyway.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to fabricate the runbook's factual backbone: it walks the skill's Required Inputs (system boundaries/ownership from the SAD, known failure modes and dependencies, SLO/RTO/RPO from the NFR, escalation contacts/on-call rotation, existing monitoring definitions), flags each as missing with a concrete way to obtain it, offers at most a skeleton with explicitly marked gaps, and warns that a runbook built on tribal knowledge ('restarting usually fixes things') fails the readiness test.
expectations: The response does not fabricate alerts, SLO/RTO/RPO targets, escalation contacts, or architecture facts; unknowns are marked as explicit gaps/TODOs, not filled in

It enumerates the skill's Required Inputs as missing: SAD-derived boundaries and ownership, known failure modes and dependencies, SLO/RTO/RPO from the NFR, escalation/on-call contacts, and existing monitoring/alerting definitions
It refuses to invent SLO/RTO/RPO values ad hoc, stating these must come from the NFR (or be formally set), per the pre-flight checklist
It flags 'restarting it usually fixes things' as tribal knowledge — the anti-pattern the runbook exists to eliminate — and requires converting it into an executable, verifiable procedure
It flags that a runbook with no alert inventory cannot satisfy 'every alert maps to a documented first action' and proposes discovering the monitoring config first

It proposes concrete discovery steps or asks targeted questions (find the SAD or document current topology, query the alerting system, identify the owning team/rotation) before the runbook can be trusted
Any skeleton offered is explicitly labeled as incomplete/not incident-ready rather than presented as a finished runbook
It notes the document still needs document control with an owner and review cadence so it doesn't rot after the compliance deadline

evals.prompt:
Here's the draft postmortem for last Tuesday's checkout outage plus the runbook snippet we used. Review both and tell me everything that's wrong before we publish:

--- POSTMORTEM: Checkout outage, Tuesday ---
Summary: Checkout was down for a while on Tuesday afternoon. Root cause: Dave from platform pushed a bad config to the API gateway without checking it; this is the second time Dave has caused an outage and it needs to be addressed in his performance review.
Timeline: it started sometime after lunch and was fixed by evening.
What went poorly: Dave's change process.
Action items: (1) be more careful with gateway configs; (2) someone should look into adding config validation someday.
Lessons: none recorded — the gateway architecture docs weren't updated since we fixed the config directly in production.

--- RUNBOOK SNIPPET USED DURING THE INCIDENT ---
Alert: GatewayErrorRateHigh — (no notes)
Procedure: if the gateway is acting up, restart it. You'll know it's recovered when things look normal again. There is no rollback step for gateway config; fix forward in prod.
evals.expected_output: A review that catches every planted defect: the postmortem names and blames an individual instead of the process that allowed the bad config; the timeline has no timestamps from detection to resolution; the root cause is a person/symptom rather than the failing mechanism and missing safeguards; both action items lack an owner and a due date (and 'be more careful' is not actionable); the architecture-relevant lesson (production config fix, stale gateway docs) was not routed through Change Management; the alert has no meaning or first action documented; the runbook step is not executable ('restart it', 'looks normal') with no verification; and there is no rollback procedure or RTO/RPO tie.
expectations: Flags the blame on a named individual ('Dave... performance review') as violating the blameless rule and requires rewriting the root cause around systems/process (no config validation, no review gate, no safe deploy path)
Flags the root cause as stopping at a person/symptom rather than the actual mechanism plus contributing factors that made the failure possible
Flags the timeline ('sometime after lunch... by evening') as missing timestamps from detection through resolution, and the summary as missing quantified customer/business impact and duration
Flags both action items as lacking an owner and a due date ('someone... someday' is a wish, not a commitment), and 'be more careful' as not an actionable system change
Flags that the lesson implying an architecture/config-management change was fixed silently in production and never routed through Change Management, leaving the gateway docs/SAD stale
Flags the GatewayErrorRateHigh alert as having no documented meaning or first action

Flags the runbook procedure as failing the readiness test: 'restart it' with 'you'll know when it looks normal' is not executable by a non-author and has no concrete verification command or success signal
Flags the absence of a rollback/recovery procedure for gateway config ('fix forward in prod') and the missing tie to any RTO/RPO or SLO target
Notes the postmortem is missing required structure such as 'What Went Well / What Went Poorly' beyond blaming a person, and contributing factors
